text:
Recent evidence supports treating sampled-negative diagnostics cautiously. [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) evaluates sampling strategies by their agreement with reference model rankings; reliability depends on sampler and sample size. A [2024 reproduction study](https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/33989) finds evaluation strategy explains much of the disagreement between popularity-bias findings. These results support comparing sampled-negative margins with full-catalog unseen-item ranks, but do not establish that margins predict useful architectural changes. [WSDM 2025 work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12008) links popularity amplification to the principal spectrum of predicted scores and representation collapse, motivating checks for popularity confounding.

Suggested protocol: construct auxiliary chronological holdouts entirely within public training histories, excluding each target from its input prefix and fitting diagnostic model copies without those targets. Compare sampled and full-catalog target ranks, stratified by item frequency and history length; measure score–popularity and embedding-norm correlations. Positive global logit scaling changes raw margins while preserving ranks, making it a useful diagnostic control. Test item normalization, popularity adjustment, and negative-sampling changes separately under matched training settings; these are proposed interventions, not established SASRec improvements. Use paired user bootstrap resampling within each category, then recompute macro-average differences and confidence intervals. User bootstraps quantify evaluation uncertainty, not training-seed variability; [paired multi-seed methodology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.19794) addresses the latter when budget permits. Preserve the pinned four-category validation HR@10 evaluator for selection. Report diagnostic GPU-seconds, users, catalog sizes, and scoring passes; full-catalog probes and ablations consume the shared search budget.
